title: Matter: Solids, Liquids and Gases
seo_title: Primary 4 Science: Matter Worksheets – Solids, Liquids and Gases (with Answers)
standard_code: Primary 4: Cycles in matter and water (Matter)
standard_text: Recognise that matter is anything that has mass and occupies space, and that it exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas. Compare the states in terms of shape and volume, and show that gases can be compressed. Measure mass and volume (summary of the MOE Primary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Primary 4 science worksheets for Singapore pupils on matter: mass and volume, solids, liquids and gases, compressing air, and measuring with a measuring cylinder. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Matter has mass and occupies space.
key_sub: Solids, liquids and gases differ in shape and volume.
body_html:
How to think about it

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Air, water and stones are matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not.

  • Solid: definite shape and definite volume.
  • Liquid: definite volume, but takes the shape of its container.
  • Gas: no definite shape or volume; fills its container and can be compressed.

Measure mass with a balance. Measure the volume of a liquid with a measuring cylinder (1 ml = 1 cm³).

Example

Water rises from 40 ml to 52 ml when a stone is added. Find the volume of the stone.

52 − 40 = 12 ml

1 ml = 1 cm³

Answer: 12 cm³.

Example

A syringe of air is sealed and pushed. Why does the plunger move in?

Air is a gas

Gases can be compressed

Answer: The air is compressed.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air has no mass. A pumped-up ball is heavier than a flat one.
  • Thinking liquids have a definite shape. They take the shape of their container.
  • Thinking light, heat or a shadow is matter. They have no mass.
  • Thinking a gas has a definite volume. It spreads out to fill its container.

faq.a: Yes. Air has mass (a pumped-up ball is heavier than a flat one) and it occupies space (it stops water filling an upside-down cup).

faq.q: What is the difference between a liquid and a gas?
faq.a: A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas has no definite shape or volume, fills its container and can be compressed.

faq.q: How do I find the volume of a stone?
faq.a: Put it in a measuring cylinder of water. The rise in the water level is the volume of the stone (1 ml = 1 cm³).

items.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: A rainbow's colours has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: Why is sand called a solid even though it can be poured?
c: Each grain has a definite shape and volume.
items.e: Many tiny solids together can be poured.

items.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: A reflection in a mirror has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: Which instrument is used to measure mass?
items.e: Mass is measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg).

items.q: Is a coin a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: A coin is a solid.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Sand has mass and occupies space.

items.q: Why is light not matter?
c: It has no mass and does not occupy space.
It moves too fast to be weighed.
items.e: Light is a form of energy.

items.q: What does 'occupies space' mean?
items.e: Two objects cannot be in the same place at the same time.

items.q: Which instrument is used to measure the volume of a liquid?
items.e: Volume is measured in ml or cm³.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Water has mass and occupies space.

items.q: Which of these is a gas?
items.e: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: A coin has mass and occupies space.

items.q: What are the three states of matter?
items.e: Matter can exist in these three states.

items.q: What is matter?
c: anything that has mass and occupies space
items.e: Air is matter even though we cannot see it.

items.q: Does air have mass?
c: Yes. A ball pumped with air is heavier than a flat ball.
items.e: Air is matter.

items.q: Which of these is a gas?
items.e: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: Heat has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: Is air a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Air is a gas.

items.q: Is liquid soap a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Why does an 'empty' bottle pushed upside down into water not fill up with water?
c: It is full of air, which occupies space.
items.e: Air takes up space.

items.q: Which of these is a gas?
items.e: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Air from a small balloon is let into a big empty box. What happens to the air?
c: It spreads out to fill the whole box.
items.e: Gases fill their container.

items.q: Why does a bicycle tyre feel hard after it is pumped?
c: The tyre is full of water.
More air has been compressed into it.
items.e: Gases can be compressed.

items.q: Is an eraser a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its shape when moved from a bowl to a plate?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which statement about gases is correct?
c: They have no definite shape and no definite volume.
items.e: A gas fills any container it is in.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid: a wooden spoon, air, sand or vinegar?
items.e: Vinegar is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter has a definite shape?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: A stone is moved from a cup to a tray. What happens to its shape and volume?
items.e: Solids have a definite shape and volume.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid: carbon dioxide, melted chocolate, sand or water vapour?
items.e: Melted chocolate is a liquid.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is a gas: butter (from the fridge), melted chocolate, orange juice or water vapour?
items.e: Water vapour is a gas.

items.q: Which state of matter fills up the whole of any container it is in?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which state of matter can be poured but cannot be compressed easily?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which has a definite volume but no definite shape?
items.e: Oil is a liquid.

items.q: Water is poured from a tall glass into a flat dish. What happens to its volume?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume.

items.q: Water is poured from a tall glass into a flat dish. What happens to its shape?
c: It stays the shape of the glass.
It changes to the shape of the dish.
It has no shape at all.
items.e: Liquids have no definite shape.

items.q: Is the gas in a balloon a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: A wooden block has mass and occupies space.

items.q: A balloon is blown up. What fills it?
items.e: The balloon gets bigger because air takes up space.

items.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Xin Yi sealed the tip of a syringe filled with water and pushed the plunger. What happened?
c: The plunger hardly moved, because water cannot be compressed easily.
The plunger moved in a lot.
items.e: Liquids have a definite volume.

items.q: Arjun weighed a flat football, then pumped air into it and weighed it again. What did Arjun find?
items.e: Air has mass.

items.q: A sealed syringe contains 30 cm³ of air. The plunger is pushed in. What happens to the volume of air?
items.e: Gases can be compressed.

items.q: Which of these can be compressed the most?
items.e: Gases can be compressed; solids and liquids hardly can.

items.q: Why is steam a gas?
c: It has no definite shape or volume and spreads out.
items.e: Steam is water in its gas state.

items.q: Why do you need to make a second hole in a can of milk to pour it out smoothly?
c: Air needs to get in to take the place of the milk.
items.e: Air and milk cannot occupy the same space.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: An ice cube has mass and occupies space.

items.q: 1 litre of water is poured into a 2-litre bottle. What is the volume of the water now?
items.e: The volume of a liquid does not change with the container.

items.q: Which state of matter can be compressed (squashed into a smaller space) easily?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 60 ml of water. When a lump of plasticine was put in, the water rose to 68 ml. Why can this method not be used for a cork?
c: A cork floats, so it does not go fully under the water.
items.e: The object must be fully under the water.

items.q: Which state of matter flows and takes the shape of its container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps the same volume but changes shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Why can a syringe of air be pushed in further than a syringe of water?
c: Air can be compressed; water cannot be compressed easily.
items.e: Gases have no definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: Light has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 70 ml of water. When a lump of plasticine was put in, the water rose to 90 ml. A second, identical lump of plasticine was added. What would the reading be?
items.e: Each one takes up 20 cm³.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 60 ml of water. When a stone was put in, the water rose to 72 ml. What is the volume of the stone?
items.e: 72 − 60 = 12 ml, and 1 ml = 1 cm³.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a use of the fact that gases can be compressed?
c: pumping air into a bicycle tyre
storing cooking gas in a cylinder
items.e: Compressed air or gas is stored in tyres and tanks.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: cooking oil, salt, shampoo or the air inside a football?
items.e: Salt grains are tiny solids.

items.q: Nurul sealed the tip of a syringe filled with air and pushed the plunger. What happened?
c: The plunger moved in a little, because air can be compressed.
The plunger could not move at all.
The air escaped through the plastic.
items.e: Gases can be compressed.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 50 ml of water. When a toy car was put in, the water rose to 55 ml. Why did the water level rise?
c: The toy car takes up space and pushes the water up.
items.e: Matter occupies space, so two things cannot be in the same place.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: A stone has mass and occupies space.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid: oxygen, steam, sugar or vinegar?
items.e: Vinegar is a liquid.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Milk has mass and occupies space.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 50 ml of water. When a stone was put in, the water rose to 60 ml. A second, identical stone was added. What would the reading be?
items.e: Each one takes up 10 cm³.

items.q: A deflated ball has a mass of 200 g. After it is pumped with air, its mass is 204 g. What does this show?
items.e: The extra mass is the mass of the air pumped in.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 60 ml of water. When a stone was put in, the water rose to 65 ml. A second, identical stone was added. What would the reading be?
items.e: Each one takes up 5 cm³.

items.q: What is air made of?
c: a mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen
items.e: About 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

items.q: Is water vapour a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Why is sand called a solid even though it pours?
c: Each grain is a solid that keeps its shape.
items.e: Look at one grain.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: A thought has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: Do gases have mass?
c: Yes, they have mass even though we cannot see most of them.
items.e: An inflated ball weighs more than a flat one.

items.q: Is honey a liquid?
c: No, it is a solid because it is thick.
Yes. It flows slowly and takes the shape of its container.
items.e: Viscous liquids flow slowly.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: What happens to a gas let out of a bottle?
c: It spreads out to fill the room.
It falls to the floor as a puddle.
items.e: Gases fill any space.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 20 g. When it is filled with water, the mass is 140 g. What is the mass of the water?
Which of these is a liquid: carbon dioxide, ice, orange juice or water vapour?
items.e: Orange juice is a liquid.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 30 g. 80 g of cooking oil is put into it. What will the balance show?
A measuring cylinder had 40 ml of water. When a glass marble was put in, the water rose to 55 ml. What is the volume of the glass marble?
items.e: 55 − 40 = 15 ml, and 1 ml = 1 cm³.

items.q: Mei Ling filled a syringe with sand and sealed the tip. She could push the plunger in a little. Why?
c: There is air between the grains of sand.
items.e: The air between the grains can be compressed.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 60 ml of water. When a stone was put in, the water rose to 75 ml. What is the volume of the stone?
items.e: 75 − 60 = 15 ml, and 1 ml = 1 cm³.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 50 ml of water. When a lump of plasticine was put in, the water rose to 58 ml. What is the volume of the lump of plasticine?
items.e: 58 − 50 = 8 ml, and 1 ml = 1 cm³.

items.q: A stone made the water in a measuring cylinder rise from 50 ml to 65 ml. A second stone made it rise from 50 ml to 58 ml. Which stone has the bigger volume?
items.e: The bigger rise means the bigger volume.

items.q: Why should the measuring cylinder be read at eye level?
items.e: Looking from above or below gives a wrong reading.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 40 g. When it is filled with sand, the mass is 140 g. What is the mass of the sand?
Ravi weighed a balloon before and after blowing it up. What was he trying to find out?
items.e: The mass increased a little, so air has mass.

items.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Why is toothpaste hard to classify?
c: It holds its shape a little but flows when squeezed, so it has properties of solids and liquids.
items.e: Some materials are tricky.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 60 ml of water. When a toy car was put in, the water rose to 75 ml. What is the volume of the toy car?
items.e: 75 − 60 = 15 ml, and 1 ml = 1 cm³.

items.q: How could you show that air takes up space?
c: Push an upside-down cup into water: the air stops the water filling it.
items.e: Gases take up space.

items.q: A measuring cylinder had 60 ml of water. When a glass marble was put in, the water rose to 65 ml. What is the volume of the glass marble?
items.e: 65 − 60 = 5 ml, and 1 ml = 1 cm³.

items.q: A sponge gets smaller when squeezed. Does this mean solids can be squashed?
c: Yes, all solids can be squashed.
No. The air in the holes is squeezed out; the solid itself does not shrink.
items.e: Think about what is in the holes.

items.q: Siti pushed an upside-down cup into a tank of water. A tissue stuck inside the cup stayed dry. Why?
c: Air in the cup occupied the space and kept the water out.
items.e: Air is matter: it occupies space.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 25 g. When it is filled with rice grains, the mass is 85 g. What is the mass of the rice grains?
An empty cup has a mass of 20 g. 120 g of sand is put into it. What will the balance show?
A pupil poured 100 ml of water into four different-shaped containers and measured the volume each time. What did she find?
c: The volume was 100 ml each time.
The volume changed with the container.
The widest container had the least water.
The tallest container had the most water.
items.e: Liquids have a definite volume.

items.q: How could you show that a gas has mass?
c: Weigh a flat football, pump it up, and weigh it again.
items.e: More air, more mass.
